idiom_name: Caffeine Cache.get(id) { key -> load(key) } + invalidate in the write path
implementation_notes: On the JVM Kotlin uses the same caches as Java: Caffeine's get(key) { key -> load(key) } (or a LoadingCache) performs the read and the populate, Kotlin's trailing-lambda syntax makes the loader read naturally, expireAfterWrite/maximumSize carry the policy, and invalidate(key) runs after the store commit. Spring's @Cacheable works identically from Kotlin with the proxy caveats of the JVM. The Kotlin standard library contains no cache, so the realization is a thin wrapper around a Java cache rather than a Kotlin-specific construct.
code_sketch:
private val cache: Cache<String, Entity> = Caffeine.newBuilder()
    .expireAfterWrite(5, TimeUnit.MINUTES)
    .maximumSize(100_000)
    .build()

fun read(id: String): Entity = cache.get(id) { key -> store.find(key) }   // populate on miss
fun update(entity: Entity) { store.save(entity); cache.invalidate(entity.id) }  // store first
pitfalls: Kotlin's non-null types do not survive the Java API: getIfPresent returns a platform type, so a miss is null and the compiler will not force the check.
A suspend function cannot be called from Caffeine's mapping lambda; use AsyncCache with a future-returning loader or the coroutine variant instead of runBlocking inside the loader.
Spring's annotation proxies and Kotlin's final-by-default classes interact: @Cacheable on a final or self-invoked method is not intercepted.

variants.name: ConcurrentHashMap + kotlinx Mutex with shared in-flight loads
variants.idiom_name: suspend cache with kotlinx.coroutines Mutex.withLock over a ConcurrentHashMap
variants.implementation_notes: For suspend-function code the concurrency primitives are Kotlin's: a ConcurrentHashMap holds the entries and a kotlinx.coroutines Mutex (withLock) or an atomic putIfAbsent of a Deferred serializes the load so concurrent callers await the same in-flight value - the coroutine analogue of single-flight. Mutex is non-reentrant and suspends, so it must never wrap a block that re-enters the cache or stalls the dispatcher; expiry, eviction and invalidation remain application code as in the dependency-free JVM form.
pitfalls: kotlinx Mutex is non-reentrant and suspends: never lock a region that calls read() again, and never use it from blocking code where runBlocking would deadlock the dispatcher.
Holding the mutex across the source-of-truth suspend call serializes every miss; scope the lock per key or share a Deferred when throughput matters.
A plain MutableMap shared between coroutines is a data race - use ConcurrentHashMap or confine the map to a single dispatcher.
